01.note: A man's wife died and left him a nursing baby, and he could not afford to pay a wet-nurse. A miracle happened: he grew breasts like a woman's and nursed his son himself. Rav Yosef said this showed how great the man was, that such a miracle was done for him; Abaye answered that, on the contrary, it showed how lowly he was, that the order of creation had to be changed for him. Rav Yehuda drew a different lesson: feeding a person is so hard that nature itself was altered, and Rav Naḥman added that miracles do happen, but food has never been created by one.
01.why: The Gemara has been discussing whether goats may go out on Shabbat with pouches on their udders, and has just told of goats in Antioch with huge udders; it attaches this related baraita about a miracle of nursing.

people.about: Sage who sees the miracle as proof of the man's greatness

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Answers Rav Yosef that the miracle shows the man's lowliness

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Sage who learns from the miracle how hard it is to provide a person's food

people.name: Rav Naḥman

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Talmud discusses.
The natural order of the world as God made it; a miracle that changes it is seen here as unusual and even undignified.

02.note: The Sages told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that young children had come to the study hall and said things not heard even in the days of Joshua bin Nun. Going through the Hebrew alphabet, they read the letters as lessons: alef-beit means 'learn wisdom', gimmel-dalet means 'give to the poor', and the gimmel's leg reaches toward the dalet because the generous run after the poor. They read the open and closed forms of letters as open and hidden teachings, and as humble righteous people who will one day be known, and the shapes of kuf and reish as God turning from the wicked while leaving an opening through which he can return.
02.why: The Gemara has been discussing the open and closed forms of letters such as mem and samekh and how old those forms are; the children's teaching gives a meaning to those letter shapes.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage to whom the report of the children's teaching is brought

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.
Several Hebrew letters (mem, nun, tzadi, peh, kaf) are written in one shape in the middle of a word and another at the end.
The life after this one, where the righteous are rewarded.

02.flag: The children's letter interpretations continue past the last STORY segment (shin and tav follow in the AFTER segments), so the story stops mid-list.

03.note: Rabbi Yosei tells of his father, Ḥalafta, who visited Rabban Gamliel in Tiberias and found him at the table of Yoḥanan HaNazuf, reading an Aramaic translation of the book of Job. Yoḥanan told Rabban Gamliel he remembered his grandfather, also Rabban Gamliel, standing on a step on the Temple Mount when a translated Job was brought to him; he told the builder to bury it under a row of bricks. Hearing this, Rabban Gamliel ordered the book buried. Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says a bowl of mortar was turned over on it, but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects: where would mortar come from on the Temple Mount, and may one destroy such writings by hand? Rather, they are left in a neglected place to decay.
03.why: Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda disagree whether holy books in translation may be rescued from a fire on Shabbat. Rav Huna says early Sages already disagreed, and Rabbi Yosei, who says they are not rescued, tells this incident.

04.note: Rav Yosef asked Rav Yosef son of Rabba which mitzva his father had been most careful about. He answered: the ritual fringes. One day, climbing the stairs, his father had a string of his fringes snap, and he would not go down until a new string was put on. Then other Sages name deeds they hope to be rewarded for. Abaye makes a feast for the Sages when a young scholar finishes a tractate. Rava does not go to sleep before searching out every argument in favor of a young scholar who comes before him for judgment. Mar bar Rav Ashi disqualifies himself from judging a young scholar, because he loves him like himself, and no one sees his own faults.
04.why: The Gemara is collecting sayings in which Sages name the mitzva they kept best and hope to be rewarded for; Rav Naḥman has just boasted of his fringes, and Rabba's fringes and these further boasts continue the list.

05.note: A certain eunuch, an apostate, taunted Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, who was bald, by asking how far it was to 'Karḥina', a pun on baldness. The rabbi answered with a pun on castration, and they traded jibes about a bald buck and a castrated goat. Seeing the rabbi without shoes, the eunuch said a man with no horse, no donkey and no shoes is worse off than the buried dead. The rabbi replied that the glory of a face is a beard, the joy of the heart is a wife, and children are God's portion, and blessed is God who denied the eunuch all three. The eunuch asked: does a bald man quarrel? The rabbi asked: does a castrated goat rebuke?
05.why: The Gemara is expounding Ecclesiastes' verses on old age and has quoted the Sages' sayings about aging bodies; it adds this exchange of insults about bodily defects before returning to old age.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
people.about: A bald Sage, taunted by the eunuch, who gives as good as he gets

terms.meaning: A Jew who has abandoned the Jewish faith.
A castrated man, who cannot grow a beard or father children.
A coin; the jibes compare the price of a bald goat and a castrated one.

06.note: Residents of the town of Kakunya asked Rav Yosef to send someone to set up an eiruv for their town. He sent Abaye, warning him to make sure there would be no outcry against it in the study hall. Abaye saw some houses that opened onto the river rather than the town and decided they could be the part left outside the eiruv. Then he changed his mind again and again: such houses do not qualify, so he would cut windows to link them; windows are unnecessary, as Rabba bar Avuh's eiruv in Meḥoza shows; that case is different, so windows are needed; and finally, windows are not needed, since a straw storehouse in Pumbedita once served as the part left out.
06.why: The mishna says a public city that became private may not have one eiruv for all of it unless a section is left out. Abaye's reversals show how hard that rule is to apply, and afterward he grasps Rav Yosef's warning.

07.note: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua went and told Rava of Abaye's ruling that Jews sharing an alleyway with a gentile could all give up their rights to one of them, who could then carry there. Rava objected that this would abolish the eiruv in that alleyway. Rav Huna answered that they could still make an eiruv as a reminder; Rava said people would then think an eiruv works even where a gentile lives. Rav Huna said they would make an announcement; Rava retorted: will you make an announcement for the children?
07.why: Abaye has just told the Jewish neighbors of a gentile to give up their rights in the alleyway to one person; this exchange rejects that solution, and Rava then offers his own: borrowing a place from the gentile.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Reports Abaye's ruling to Rava and defends it

people.name: Rava
people.about: Raises objection after objection to the ruling

terms.meaning: A legal arrangement that joins homes into one shared domain so that carrying is permitted on Shabbat; a gentile resident who has not rented out his share blocks it.
Renouncing one's share in a shared space for Shabbat, so that others may carry there.

08.note: A baby's warm water for his Shabbat circumcision had spilled, and Rava offered to give up his rights to his own courtyard so water could be carried over from it. Ravina challenged him: didn't Shmuel say rights cannot be given up from one courtyard to another? Rava said he followed Rabbi Yoḥanan on that. Ravina asked why, then, Rava did not stay where he was, give up his rights, and have the others give theirs back to him afterward, as Rav allows. Rava said that on this he followed Shmuel, who forbids it. Ravina pressed that both rulings rest on one reason; Rava answered that Shmuel's reason here is different: so that the Sages' rules do not become a joke.
08.why: The Gemara has been telling of spilled circumcision water on Shabbat; Rava's plan leads into the question whether rights can be given up and given back, which the Gemara then takes up as a dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

people.name: Ravina

09.note: Ulla was staying at the house of Rav Menashe on Shabbat when a man came and knocked on the door. Ulla said: Who is that? May his body be desecrated, since he desecrates Shabbat. Rabba told him the Sages forbade only musical sounds on Shabbat, not knocking. Abaye raised an objection to Rabba from a teaching that allows drawing wine with a siphon and dripping water for a sick person on Shabbat; the answer does not come within the story.
09.why: After the mishna's ruling on drawing water from the Cistern of the Exiles on Shabbat, the Gemara turns to whether making a sound on Shabbat is forbidden; Ulla's curse and Rabba's reply open that debate.

10.note: Yoḥanan ben Narbbai and his household were said to eat three hundred calves, drink three hundred jugs of wine and eat forty se'a of doves for dessert, so that in his days no sacrificial meat was ever left over. As for Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai: a king and queen argued whether goat or lamb is better and asked the High Priest. Yissakhar waved his hand in contempt and said that if goat were better, it would be the daily offering. The king, angered at his lack of respect, ordered his right hand cut off. Yissakhar bribed the official, who cut off his left; when the king heard, he had the right cut off too. Rav Yosef blessed God for punishing Yissakhar in this world.
10.why: The Gemara has listed the cries raised in the Temple courtyard against unworthy priests and for worthy ones, including Yissakhar and Yoḥanan ben Narbbai; this tells what each man was like and how Yissakhar ended.

people.name: Yoḥanan ben Narbbai

people.name: Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai

11.note: Rav Huna son of Rav Natan visited the house of Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak. Asked his name, he said 'Rav Huna', title and all. Invited to sit on the couch, he sat at once; offered a cup, he took it the first time, drank it in two sips, and did not turn his face away. His hosts asked about each act. He said he had always been called by that name; that a guest does whatever the host says, except leave; that one may refuse a lesser person but not a great one; that drinking a cup in one gulp is greedy, in two is good manners and in three is haughty; and that only a bride turns her face.
11.why: The mishna says that a bride eating the Passover offering with a group turns her face away, out of embarrassment; Rav Huna cites that rule to explain why he, not being a bride, did not turn his.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Natan
people.about: The guest whose behavior surprises his hosts

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage whose house Rav Huna visits

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna; Rav Huna quotes one on how to drink a cup.
The early code of Jewish law the Talmud discusses; here, its rule about a bride.

12.note: When Rabbi Akiva was in prison, Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai asked him to teach him Torah, and Rabbi Akiva refused. Rabbi Shimon joked that he would tell his father Yoḥai to turn Rabbi Akiva over to the government. Rabbi Akiva answered that the cow wants to nurse even more than the calf wants to suck; Rabbi Shimon replied that it is the calf that is in danger. Rabbi Akiva then gave him five teachings: if you would hang yourself, hang from a tall tree; teach your son from a corrected text; do not cook in a pot your fellow cooked in; eating fruit without payment is a mitzva and good for the body; and marrying a wife is a mitzva that keeps the body pure and brings children.
12.why: The Gemara has just quoted seven pieces of advice Rabbi Akiva gave his son; it adds the five he gave Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, then moves on to similar instructions Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave his sons.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Imprisoned teacher who gives Rabbi Shimon five teachings

people.about: Asks Rabbi Akiva to teach him Torah while he is in prison

people.name: Yoḥai

The Gemara explains this as lending money against land and eating its produce, which helps both lender and borrower.

13.note: The wicked kingdom decreed that the Jews must not study Torah, must not circumcise their sons, and must desecrate Shabbat. Yehuda ben Shammua and his colleagues went for advice to a certain matron whom all the leading men of Rome visited. She told them to cry out at night. They went and cried out: O Heavens! Are we not your brothers, children of one father and one mother? How are we different from every other nation, that you issue harsh decrees against us? The decrees were annulled, and that day, the twenty-eighth of Adar, was made a festive day.
13.why: The Gemara is asking whether Megillat Ta'anit has been cancelled. Rav Tovi bar Mattana objects with this festive day, added after the Temple's destruction: no one adds days to a list that was cancelled.

people.name: Yehuda ben Shammua
people.about: Leads his colleagues to seek advice and cry out against the decree

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Mattana
people.about: Cites this festive day in the Gemara's debate

terms.meaning: An ancient list of days of rejoicing on which fasting is forbidden.
A noble Roman lady.
The text's name for the hostile ruling power, here Rome.

14.note: Rav had offended Rabbi Ḥanina by not restarting a Torah reading for him, and for thirteen years Rav came to him every Yom Kippur eve to ask forgiveness, but Rabbi Ḥanina refused. The Gemara asks how Rav could ask more than three times, against the teaching of Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, and answers that Rav was different. It then asks how Rabbi Ḥanina could refuse, when Rava taught that whoever lets go of his honor is forgiven his sins. The answer: Rabbi Ḥanina had dreamed that Rav was hung on a palm tree, a sign that he would become head of an academy, so he refused to be appeased, so that Rav would go and study Torah in Babylonia.
14.why: The Gemara has been telling how Rav sought forgiveness from people on Yom Kippur eve; these questions explain why Rav kept asking and why Rabbi Ḥanina kept refusing, before it turns to the laws of confession on that day.

15.note: Reish Lakish said: I am the atonement for Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons. When the Torah was forgotten in the Land of Israel, Ezra came up from Babylonia and reestablished it; when it was forgotten again, Hillel the Babylonian came up and reestablished it; when it was forgotten yet again, Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons came up and reestablished it. He then cites their ruling: Rabbi Dosa and the Rabbis agreed that the mats of Usha can become ritually impure and those of Tiberias cannot, and disagreed only about mats from other places.
15.why: The Gemara is asking what the word ḥotzalot means. Reish Lakish says it means plain mats, and this tribute introduces the teaching of Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons on which that view rests.

16.note: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai was brought a cooked dish to taste, and Rabban Gamliel was brought two dates and a bucket of water, and each said: take them up to the sukka. But when Rabbi Tzadok was given less than an egg-bulk of food, he took it in a cloth, ate it outside the sukka, and did not say a blessing after it.
16.why: The previous mishna allows a snack outside the sukka, so the Gemara asks why this one tells a story that seems to contradict it; it answers that one may choose to be strict, then weighs Rabbi Tzadok's case against Rav Yosef and Abaye.

17.note: Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yitzḥak sat at a meal. Rav Naḥman asked for a teaching; Rabbi Yitzḥak said one may not talk while eating, lest one choke. After the meal he taught, in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name, that Jacob our father did not die. Rav Naḥman asked whether he was eulogized, embalmed and buried for nothing; Rabbi Yitzḥak said he was interpreting a verse. He also said anyone who says 'Rahab, Rahab' at once has a seminal emission; Rav Naḥman said it did not affect him, and Rabbi Yitzḥak said he meant those who knew her. Parting, Rav Naḥman asked for a blessing. Rabbi Yitzḥak told of a traveler who blessed a tree that its saplings be like it, and blessed him: may your offspring be like you.

people.about: Teaches Rav Naḥman and blesses him when they part

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Sage in whose name Rabbi Yitzḥak teaches

A short illustrative story used to make a point.

18.note: Ilfa and Rabbi Yoḥanan studied Torah together and grew very poor, so they set out to go into business. Sitting under a crumbling wall eating bread, Rabbi Yoḥanan heard two ministering angels: one wanted to knock the wall down and kill them for leaving eternal life for passing life; the other said to leave them, since one had his time still ahead. Ilfa heard nothing, so Rabbi Yoḥanan concluded the future was his and went back. Ilfa went on, and by his return Rabbi Yoḥanan led the academy. Told he too would have led had he stayed, Ilfa hung from a ship's mast, vowing to fall and drown if he could not answer any question on certain baraitot from the Mishna. An old man posed a case about a will, and Ilfa answered.
18.why: The Gemara presents this as another story involving an unstable wall, and follows it with one about a house that collapses the moment Naḥum of Gam Zu is carried out.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: Rabbi Yoḥanan's study partner, who goes into business and later proves his learning

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Hears the angels, returns to study, and becomes head of the academy

terms.meaning: Angels who serve God; here two of them debate whether to kill the two men.

Coins; the text says a sela is double a shekel.

19.note: Most of Adar had passed with no rain, and the people asked Ḥoni HaMe'aggel to pray. He prayed, and no rain fell. He drew a circle, stood in it, and swore by God's name not to move until God had mercy on His children. Rain trickled; he asked for rain to fill the cisterns, and it poured in huge drops; he asked for rain of blessing, and it fell normally until the people fled to the Temple Mount. Asked to pray it away, he said one does not pray over too much good, yet he offered a thanks-offering bull and prayed, and the sun came out. Shimon ben Shetaḥ sent word that he would have excommunicated him, were he not Ḥoni, who nags God like a son his father and gets his way.
19.why: The mishna mentioned in passing that the people sent to Ḥoni for rain; the Gemara now gives the full account, after discussing rain that comes in its season and sin that holds it back.

people.about: Sage who rebukes Ḥoni but cannot punish him

20.note: Rav taught that each day a heavenly voice proclaims that the whole world is fed for the sake of Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, yet he lives on a kav of carobs from one Shabbat eve to the next. Every Friday his wife heated the oven and made smoke, out of embarrassment, so no one would know they had nothing to bake. A malicious neighbor, suspicious, knocked on the door, and the embarrassed wife went into an inner room. A miracle happened: the neighbor saw the oven full of bread and the kneading basin full of dough, and called to her to bring a shovel before her bread burned. The wife answered that she had gone in for just that, and a tanna taught that she was used to miracles.
20.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's prayers stopped and restarted the rain, and continues with more wonders done for him and his family.

people.about: A righteous man for whose sake the world is fed, though he lives on almost nothing

people.name: Rav
people.about: Teaches about the heavenly voice, as reported by Rav Yehuda

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports Rav's teaching

terms.meaning: A voice from heaven announcing God's word.

A Sage of the early period whose teachings are quoted in the Talmud.
